claims.text: The homogenized, solution-treated HfNbTaTiZr starting material is a single-phase solid solution with minimal segregation and precipitates.
Short-range chemical order forms in homogenized HfNbTaTiZr at elevated temperatures.
The short-range-order zones form within a BCC lattice.
Short-range chemical order increases lattice friction and restricts dislocation glide.
Restricted dislocation mobility produces higher elevated-temperature strength than in the as-cast state.
Elevated-temperature short-range ordering stabilizes the lattice.
Short-range ordering reduces the thermal expansion of homogenized HfNbTaTiZr relative to as-cast HfNbTaTiZr.
The thermal expansion coefficient of the homogenized alloy is 5–10% lower than that of the as-cast alloy from 800 to 1300 °C.
The homogenized alloy retains more stiffness at elevated temperature than the as-cast alloy.
The homogenized alloy has a near-isotropic elastic response and less elastic anisotropy than the as-cast alloy.
The homogenized alloy exhibits more uniform elevated-temperature stress–strain behavior than the as-cast alloy.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr has higher thermal expansion than homogenized HfNbTaTiZr.
Less uniform atomic distributions in the as-cast alloy cause more pronounced elastic anisotropy.
The proposed mechanism applies only while HfNbTaTiZr remains a single-solution BCC phase without significant second-phase formation or large interstitial content.
The proposed upper-temperature validity limit is approximately 1300 °C.
A strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1 is suitable for the controlled elevated-temperature comparison.
In situ diffraction under load can determine temperature-dependent lattice strains, elastic anisotropy, and elastic moduli in a refractory BCC high-entropy alloy.
Atomistic simulations can characterize high-temperature short-range ordering and local pair probabilities in a high-entropy alloy.
Processing variations may change the magnitude of local ordering and the resulting mechanical and thermal responses.
